section.title: Increasing and decreasing functions
section.p: A speedometer does not only tell how fast a car is moving. Its sign tells the direction of motion. Positive velocity means position is increasing. Negative velocity means position is decreasing.
The same idea works for any differentiable function.

subsection.title: Increasing and decreasing functions
subsection.p: The motion example suggests the general language.

statement.p: Let f be a function on an interval I.
The function f is increasing on I if, whenever x_1\lt x_2 in I, we have
The function f is decreasing on I if, whenever x_1\lt x_2 in I, we have

subsection.p: Increasing means that moving to the right on the input line moves upward on the graph. Decreasing means that moving to the right moves downward on the graph.
A function can increase on one interval and decrease on another. The function s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t is increasing on [0,1] and on [3,4], but decreasing on [1,3]. The intervals matter.

subsection.title: The first derivative sign rule
subsection.p: The examples point to the rule we want.

statement.p: Suppose f is continuous on an interval I and differentiable at the interior points of I.
throughout the interior of I, then f is increasing on I.
throughout the interior of I, then f is decreasing on I.

subsection.p: This rule is one of the most useful tools in differential calculus. Its proof will come from the Mean Value Theorem in . For now, the meaning is visible from local linear approximation:
When h\gt 0, moving to the right by a small amount, a positive f'(x) gives a positive change in f. A negative f'(x) gives a negative change in f.
The Mean Value Theorem will explain why this local information controls the whole interval.

subsection.p: The method has a simple rhythm.

principle.title: Making a first derivative sign chart

li.p: Find where f'(x)=0 or where f'(x) does not exist.
Use those numbers to split the domain into intervals.
Test the sign of f'(x) on each interval.
Translate f'\gt 0 into increasing, and f'\lt 0 into decreasing.

subsection.p: The derivative does not need to be drawn. The sign chart may contain all the information we need.

subsection.title: Critical numbers
subsection.p: The numbers where the derivative is zero or undefined deserve a name.

statement.p: Let c be a number in the domain of f. We call c a critical number of f if

subsection.p: The phrase in the domain of f matters. A function can only have a critical number at an input where the function itself is defined.
For f(x)=x^3-3x, the critical numbers are -1 and 1.
For g(x)=|x|, the number 0 is a critical number because g'(0) does not exist. The graph has a corner there.

figure.caption: For g(x)=|x|, the derivative is undefined at 0. So 0 is a critical number.

subsection.p: A critical number is a candidate for an important point on the graph. It is not a promise.
For example, h(x)=x^3 has derivative h'(x)=3x^2. So h'(0)=0. The number 0 is critical. But h(x)=x^3 keeps increasing through 0. It does not turn around there.

note.title: Key take-away
note.p: Critical numbers are candidates, not conclusions.

subsection.p: The next section asks which critical numbers actually give high points or low points.
